You are lying in bed, perfectly still.
But in truth, you have never really stopped.
The Earth is carrying you, racing around the Sun.
The Sun carries the Earth around the center of the Milky Way.
And in the vaster void, the whole Milky Way, with dozens of neighboring galaxies, is moving steadily toward one direction in deep space.
At more than six hundred kilometers per second.
In eight hours of quiet sleep, you travel eighteen million kilometers through the universe.
We can sense this journey because of an ancient light that fills the sky.
The afterglow of the newborn universe, over billions of years, became the microwave background spread evenly across the heavens.
Yet precise satellites caught an extremely faint difference in temperature —
Ahead of us the microwaves are slightly compressed, three thousandths of a degree warmer; behind us, slightly cooler.
This tiny dipole, like a headwind, points precisely to where we are heading.
Deep in that direction, what could be pulling us?
The universe is expanding. All galaxies should drift apart, like leaves carried downstream.
This is called the Hubble flow.
But above this great current, wherever a huge mass gathers, its gravity acts like an unseen whirlpool, gently tugging at nearby galaxies.
Astronomers call this extra drift on top of the expansion "peculiar velocity".
Measuring the peculiar velocities of thousands of galaxies is like scattering handfuls of leaves across the universe.
Follow where the leaves drift, and the river of gravity shows its course.
In 1987, seven astronomers published the results of years of measurements.

From the distances and velocities of hundreds of elliptical galaxies, they found to their surprise that vast groups of galaxies, across hundreds of millions of light-years, were all streaming toward the depths of the southern sky.
At nearly six hundred kilometers per second, heading straight for the constellation Norma.
These seven astronomers came to be known as the "Seven Samurai".
And that unknown source, hidden in deep space and pulling on countless galaxies, was given a name —
The Great Attractor.
Yet seeing the Great Attractor clearly is extremely hard.
When we look along the pull of gravity, our view is blocked squarely by the disk of our own Milky Way.
Hundreds of billions of stars, and thick interstellar dust and gas, hide nearly a fifth of the sky.
Astronomers call this blind spot the "Zone of Avoidance".
It blocks visible light, but not the more penetrating infrared and radio waves.
Astronomers turned to sharper wavelengths, piercing the Milky Way's haze bit by bit.
In 1996, radio and infrared surveys finally broke through the dust and counted many hidden galaxies more than two hundred million light-years away.
At the heart of Norma sits an exceptionally massive galaxy cluster — Abell 3627.
It gathers hundreds of galaxies, with the mass of a thousand trillion suns: one of the heaviest gravitational hubs in the nearby universe.
But careful orbital calculations showed that this one cluster alone could never pull the whole flood of galaxies.
The true outline of the Great Attractor is far grander than a single cluster.
As the data grew to tens of thousands of galaxies, the three-dimensional flow of the universe was reconstructed.
Just as geographers trace river basins by the flow of water, astronomers mapped the gravitational borders of the streaming galaxies.
The vast basin we live in spans five hundred million light-years and holds a hundred thousand large galaxies.
It was named — Laniakea.
In Hawaiian, it means "immeasurable heaven".
The Milky Way is just a small boat drifting downstream in this wide basin.
Look even deeper, and the picture of the universe unfolds further.

Three times farther than the Great Attractor sleeps the even larger Shapley Supercluster; deeper in the Zone of Avoidance lies the Vela Supercluster, eight hundred million light-years away. All of them exert a distant pull.
And in the opposite direction, behind us, stretches a vast void hundreds of millions of light-years wide.
Galaxies there are very sparse, and gravity is far below average. The stronger gravity around it pulls matter outward, as if an invisible force were gently pushing us from behind.
One side pulls, the other pushes.
In recent years, more precise cosmic simulations and distance measurements have brought new reflection.
The latest dynamical reconstructions show that even all the massive structures nearby explain only about seventy percent of our speed, and the direction is still off by more than thirty degrees.
Some scientists even suggest there may never have been a single, solid "Great Attractor".
The long current we feel is the combined pull of countless masses and voids — near and far, bright and dark.
Of course, other recent distance surveys still see gravity flowing toward a common point.
The Great Attractor may be just a silhouette of gravity, overlapping as seen from our particular place.
It's late.
Your room, the shadows of trees outside, the whole city, even this blue planet — all are moving calmly through this vast web of gravity.
At this scale, there is nothing you need to worry about.
Whatever pulls ahead, whatever pushes behind,
on this long and quiet journey, tonight will pass gently.
Sleep now.
Good night.
